comments.text:
@adamsewell7878  In regards to whether it's better to get AMD or Intel with an AMD gpu, it doesn't really make a difference, they should both work fine and have resizeable bar/smart access memory (which is a feature you should enable in your BIOS).

Performance-wise, judging by reviews they seem pretty similar, with Intel edging out in productivity, while AMD has less power consumption, and them pretty much neck-and-neck for gaming.

So in the end it comes down to price, it seems the AMD CPU is cheaper, but needs a more expensive motherboard (because it's a new platform) and ddr5 ram, while Intel has some motherboards that can use ddr4. On the flip side, AMD should have longer motherboard support, making it easy to upgrade down the line.
If you're in the US, I'd recommend checking out Microcenter, they have great cpu and motherboard combo deals, and I'd go with whichever you can find for cheaper. If they come out to the same price, I'd personally go with AMD just because of the longer motherboard support and lower power usage, but if you do a lot of productivity work Intel would be a better fit.

Hope this helps!

comments.text:
I think one of the worst scams of the GPU world was the GeForce 5 series, er – I mean “FX” series. (NVidia skipped “5” for some dumb reason).  Let’s go back to 2003 and even 2002.  Yep, 20 years ago!   The GeForce 3ti and GeForce 4ti series were awesome cards.

The Geforce 4 scams = NVidia pretty much re-labels a bunch of GF2 cards into the MX400 and MX4000 low-end series. ($50~120 cards) They are NV17/18 cards (GF2), so Nvidia would have a “new” low-end line of cards to sell that required NO R&D.  GF3 was NV20, GF4 TI was NV25/NV28 (NV28 = AGP 8x = meh). 

Now the GF2 MX200 was a very popular little entry card, much better than the TNT2, and of course, were upgraded over the now dead 3DFx Voodoo 3 cards.  67fps vs 46fps in 1024x768 16bit color with Quake 3.  The GF2 GTS was a $150+ card back then, was OEM/poor man’s version of the $200+ top-end GF2-Pro.  A few FPS slower at $75 less.

Anyway, the MX420, and MX440 performed about the same as the GF2 MX200 and GF2 GTS at slightly lower pricing.  People bought them thinking they were getting GF4 feature sets. Nope, as they’re 100% GF2 technology.  By 2003, they were useless for gaming.
Gamers that knew better would have bought the TI4200 ($180 64mb, $200 128 MB). The 4400 ($300) and 4600 ($400) were higher-clocked versions and not worth it. These were the high-end GPUs of that era.

The GeForce 5 Scams = Where to start?  FX series was their real-time 3D movie-quality cards in 2003.  The launch card was the FX 5800, the world’s first  HUGE dual-slot video card.  Really, people were complaining it was a HUGE card with a loud blower.  On top of that, its MSRP was like $600, outrageous!  And people were paying $1000+ to get their hands on them, the world’s first DX9 card!   The card wasn’t worth it.  The DX8 games weren’t much better.  Months later, Nvidia would release the GF5200 and 5600 as their lower/mid-range cards.  They were a joke at $150 and $200, respectively.   The 5200 came in various flavors of junk, with the end-user at the mercy of the 3rd party maker on what they’re getting.
In general, people were buying the 5200, thinking they were better than the 4200, but in fact, were about half as fast, at best.   The $200 5600 Ultra was easily slower than the older Ti4200 selling for $130~150!     These 5000 series cards ran hot and low performance, they were a joke and that’s when ATI (before AMD bought them out) gained a lot of ground with the 9200, 9500, and 9700 cards. 

It would take Nvidia over a year to fix the 5000 series with the 5500 (bottom end), 5700 (mid-range), and 5900.   The much cheaper 5700 ($200) was faster than the 5800.   This era was Nvidia's first colossal embarrassment.  
Side Story: In a tech support group.  A member bought a GF-5200 (non-Ultra, which is half as fast as the 5200 ultra on a good day) from Walmart but was confused when his PC booted up and said, “GF TI4200”.  Apparently, someone did a switch with Walmart, swapping out the card for a refund.   Everyone told that guy he was LUCKY to accidentally pay $100 for a used card!  We told him to KEEP the card.  There was nothing wrong with it.  

 We, of course, laughed at the scammer who down-graded their gaming rig!   He had to have been confused as to why all his games were running horribly.   LOL!!

So, how does this shared memory on consoles work? .. because - when you say that the PS5 has 16gb of shared memory - that would be system memory PLUS video memory.

Looking at my resource monitor - i will use Cyberpunk 2077 as an example (while also running Youtube on another monitor, Photoshop Palettes on a 3rd and having the Cintiq pro connected as a 4th screen)

result: 
- 15.8/64GB system ram usage 
- 13.8/24GB video ram usage

that makes 29.6gb ram if it was shared ... 

I am well aware that consoles are more efficient with their shared ram .. but still, i am currently on almost 30gb ram in use .. nearly twice as much as the PS5 can do. 

Furthermore, i read that off of the 16GB ram that the PS5 has .. it uses around 2GB for system files - - leaving 14gb for video ram and normal ram

So, why is 8GB not enough on video cards when it is purely, non shared 8gb ... with the normal recommended ram (16gb) for a gaming PC, that should amount to 24 gb of "shared" ram


edit: i am well aware that it clearly shows that i am using a lot more than 8gb video ram (so yes, i know that 8gb is not enough .. for that game, on that detail level) - but if we take the consoles as the main culprit for jacking up the video ram, it does not really make sense to me.

comments.text:
Said this durring the 4060Ti review, will say it again.
The VRAM problem (Hopefully) is a red herring/misnomer which is moreso growing pains in the industry.

The current Geometry Shading paragidm (with one full-detail Level-of-Detail 0 model, with multiple LODs progressing to a persistent background LOD), is just getting stretched to it's limit with how much LOD devs are putting into games like TLOUP1, Jedi Survivor, Hogwarts Legacy

This is overextering the VRAM of many GPUs because with the extreme LOD models and LOD-Dense scenes we are getting in games like the aforementioned titles, you need far more LOD-Tiers to make a smooth detail graident into the background before reaching the PLOD. 

So, say a model would take a megabyte at most without textures in the early PS4/Xbone days. Nowadays they may be breaching the >10MB limit per-model.

Heck, Stranger of Paradise: Final Fantasy Origin more or less had a foreshadow of this problem with them just unoptimizing their models and not having many LOD teirs at all with 30mbs of geometric data per common enemy model in some instances (Thus why the game overwhelmed VRAM on PC and could run a lot better if you turned off hair XD)


The solution of this problem already is in place however, just look at Fornite's big UE5 Update.

That version of Fornite, with the Nanite Compute Geometry feature enabled, has an extreme degree of geometric density and LOD, primarily due to EVERY SINGLE BLADE OF GRASS BEING A MODEL. Yet, VRAM isn't that big of a issue when Nanite is engaged.

This is because Compute Geometry/Mesh Shading dynamically adjusts the detail of the model in runtime, effectively "creating" LOD tiers on it's own based on the camera's view.

Therefore, with Nanite/Compute Geo/Mesh Shading, you only need 2 Models per model in a game, the Full-Res LOD which would get dynamically adjusted via Nanite, then the PLOD which Nanite will automatically produce a gradient towards due to how it works.

So you are reducing file sizes and VRAM cost of a scene from needing, 4,5,6+ versions of a model loaded in to switch between in case of character distance/travel, down to 2.
comments.author: @Alovon

comments.text: That's incredibly interesting, thanks for sharing. If fortnite has implemented that solution, how long do you think it will take before everyone else does the same? Or is it less possible with more realistic art styles.

comments.text:
Unfortunately I don't think it's going to go the way you hope it is. I looked up a bunch of benchmarks comparing DX11 and 12 for Fortnite and in general DX12 uses more VRAM than DX11. I could not confirm if Nanites were turned on however. I think the idea for nanites is that they will allow more to be added to games rather than just adding performance. 

The reality is that next gen games are going to take a lot of VRAM and 8GB just isn't enough. That said, It is enough for Fortnite, I was shocked at how little vram Fortnite actually uses, but Fortnite isn't the type of game that pushes those type of boundaries
comments.author: @chronometer9931

comments.text:
@chronometer9931  Nanite by nature should reduce the VRAM allocation per model as it's reducing the number of models.

Now, if Nanite does take more VRAM in Fortnite at this point, it should be marginal becuase the budget saved by eliminating the LOD levels between LOD0 and PLOD was re-spent in increasing geometric density.

The overall point I was making was an incredibly geometry dense scene without Nanite would take a lot more VRAM than the same scene with Nanite/Compute Geometry

Pretty much push the VRAM cost "Clock" back a bit. It will continue to rise unless Epic/NV/AMD come up with a way to completely eliminate PLODs and fully bank on Compute Geometry or other ways of reducing VRAM usage for textures/geo. But the point is until we hit next generation things should stabilize for a while once developers shift to Nanite/Mesh Shading/Compute Geo

comments.text:
@tumultoustortellini  the effect actually should scale better with realistic art, Nanite is fully compute driven based on the performance target in question so it will reduce geometry complexity in the distance more aggressively within it's capability to try to help performance.

As for when, well I hope any proper UE5 release uses Nanite as it'd be a bit dumb to not. As for non-UE5 games, I do think that developers will try to make their own compute geometry solutions or switch to Mesh Shading which is pretty much the same thing but at the hardware level
